children: Warsh revived the dollar with a hawkish Jackson Hole speech. Friday’s payroll numbers now decide whether that rate-hike warning has economic support.
Euro meets a newly confident dollar
The
pair traded near $1.16 Monday after the dollar climbed toward a two-week high from around $1.18 last week.
The euro is still heading for a second consecutive monthly gain, but its momentum weakened after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh reminded markets that US interest rates may need to rise again.

At Jackson Hole, Warsh said further tightening could be required unless inflation moves convincingly toward the Fed’s 2% target. Traders now assign roughly a 57% probability to a September rate increase, up sharply from about 35% before his speech.

Two-year Treasury yields rose toward 4.33%, increasing the return available on dollar assets. That yield advantage is the major pair’s immediate problem: the euro can have improving economic data, but it must compete with a currency whose central bank is again threatening to pay investors more.
Friday’s jobs report gets the deciding vote

August nonfarm payrolls arrive Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET, with economists expecting approximately 50,000 new jobs and unemployment to remain near 4.1%. That follows July’s surprise loss of 23,000 positions.
A stronger report — particularly firm payrolls, wages and hours worked — would support Warsh’s case and could push the euro deeper below $1.16.
Another weak reading would challenge September hike expectations, pressure Treasury yields and give the pair a cleaner route back toward recent highs.

Traders should watch the supporting evidence first. US job openings arrive Tuesday, while private-sector employment indicators, unemployment claims and revised productivity data provide additional clues later in the week.
Europe brings inflation of its own

Eurozone inflation arrives Tuesday and may show the headline rate accelerating toward 3.3%. Hotter inflation would strengthen expectations that the European Central Bank raises rates in September, potentially offsetting some of the dollar support produced by Warsh.

Final manufacturing and services PMIs will test whether the region’s recent improvement is durable. August’s preliminary survey showed eurozone business activity expanding at its fastest pace this year, helped by stronger manufacturing orders and renewed export growth.
On the chart, $1.1600 is the immediate pivot, followed by support around $1.1550 and $1.1500. Resistance sits near $1.1660–$1.1700.
A soft US jobs report plus firm eurozone inflation could force a break higher; strong payrolls would leave euro bulls negotiating with both the Fed and the bond market.
